savings_track.why: Of 100 households like yours, about 15 (7–30) will have an income gap of more than 3 months in the next 10 years. The goal is about 2.5 months of expenses (about $17,500); you have 4 months saved. You already have enough saved for this goal. This is a savings goal, kept separate from the supplies budget.

requirements.plain: 2 battery lights: a headlamp or lantern for each person aged 4 and over. Use lights, not candles. (Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)
1 pack of AA or AAA batteries for the lights and the radio: one pack lasts a household about 7 days. Check which sizes your lights use. (Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)

1 battery power station (about 1,070 Wh each) to keep refrigerated medicine cold in a small cooler. Your essential load (phones) is about 30 Wh a day, 210 Wh for 7 days; one station gives about 910 Wh after losses, enough for about 30.3 days of that load. A full-size fridge alone would drain one in about 0.9 days. (retail prices, ENERGY STAR, Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)

Optional: a portable generator can run the fridge and lights through a 7-day outage. It must run outdoors, at least 20 feet from windows, doors and vents, never in a garage, and it needs fuel (see the fuel line). (CDC, Ready.gov, Ready Reckoner research; some amounts are estimates)

Optional for a 7-day outage: a portable solar panel with a battery. In December a 100 W panel near your latitude makes about 382 Wh a day (like Miami, FL (Phoenix, AZ makes 424)). Your essential load of about 30 Wh a day needs about 10 W of panels in full sun; a full-size fridge would need about 260 W. Panels laid flat or in shade make less. (NREL PVWatts, ENERGY STAR; some amounts are estimates)

Optional: keeping a fridge running takes about 995 Wh a day (a chest freezer about 597) × 7 days = 6,970 Wh. A closed fridge keeps food cold about 4 hours and a full freezer about 48; shelf-stable food avoids the need. (ENERGY STAR, Ready.gov)

For a boil-water notice of up to 7 days: make about 5.1 gallons of drinking water safe each day, about 35.4 gallons in all. To make it safe, boil it for 1 minute (3 minutes above 5,000 feet), or add 8 drops of 6 % unscented bleach per gallon (6 drops of 8.25 %) and wait 30 minutes; double the bleach for cloudy or very cold water. A gas stove can boil water while the gas flows; never use a camp stove or grill indoors. (Ready.gov, CDC, NCA5 Atlas, AAP; some amounts are estimates)

1 bottle of plain unscented bleach (5 to 9 % sodium hypochlorite, not the splashless kind), for making water safe and for cleaning, however long your target is. At about 0.5 mL a gallon, each ounce treats about 60 gallons of clear water (30 if it is cloudy or very cold), so one bottle treats thousands of gallons. Bleach weakens in storage: buy a fresh bottle every 6 months, when you replace the water you store yourself. (CDC, EPA; some amounts are estimates)

If you boil on a camp stove outdoors, about 4.9 lb of propane brings 134 L to a boil (about 25 to 30 L a pound). Never use a camp stove indoors, and keep no more than 2 one-pound cylinders inside. (EIA, local fire code, CDC; some amounts are estimates)

3 people × 1.75 gallons a day × 3 days = 15.8 gallons, plus 0.8 gallons to mix formula, plus 0.9 gallons for the dog: about 17.4 gallons. Your county has at least 30 days a year at 95 °F or more, and drinking water can double in heat, so each person gets 1.75 gallons a day. Replace water you store yourself every 6 months. (Ready.gov, CDC, NCA5 Atlas, AAP; some amounts are estimates)

Free first step: fill clean drink bottles you already have with tap water, about 6 gallons, the most a household can usually gather this way. Not milk jugs: they leak. Label them and replace the water every 6 months. (Ready Reckoner research, CDC, Ready.gov, Church of Jesus Christ; some amounts are estimates)
A two-bucket toilet for when toilets can't flush: 2 sturdy buckets with a seat, one for pee and one for poo. (RDPO, Oregon OEM)

Toilet bags: about 0.45 heavy garbage bags a person a day (0.3 to 0.6), counting both bags of a double-bagged load: 2 people × 3 days = 3 bags. Fill halfway, tie, double-bag, and store away from food, water, children and pets. Don't put them in curbside trash or bury them unless officials say so. (RDPO, Oregon OEM; some amounts are estimates)

Cover material for the poo bucket (sawdust, shredded paper, dry leaves or pet bedding): about 1 cup a person a day (0.5 to 1.5) × 2 people × 3 days = 6 cups, about 0.4 gallons. (RDPO; some amounts are estimates)

2 adults at about 2,262 kcal a day each: about 4,523 kcal a day × 10 days = 45,200 kcal. These are moderately active needs; the form does not ask sex, so men's and women's needs are averaged. Count calories, not servings. Babies under 1 are fed breast milk or formula (see the formula line). (Dietary Guidelines)

As everyday groceries: about $186 for 20 person-days (USDA Thrifty Food Plan, $8.44 a person a day, plus 10 % for a household of 2). Buy what you already eat, keep it in the pantry and use the oldest first. (USDA)

As bulk staples such as wheat, rice and beans: about $50 ($2.15 to $2.85 a person a day). Cheapest, but it needs cooking and is short on some vitamins, so it suits months rather than days. (Church of Jesus Christ, BYU)

As freeze-dried or dehydrated meals: about $543 ($9 to $39 per 2,000 kcal, so $204 to $882). They need about 0.6 gallons of extra water a person a day to prepare. (Dietary Guidelines, retail prices; some amounts are estimates)

A retail "30-day" food kit supplies about 1,290 to 1,730 kcal a day. For the average person here (about 2,262 kcal a day) one lasts about 17 to 23 days, not 30. Compare kits by total kcal. (Dietary Guidelines, retail prices)

1 baby on formula: up to 32 oz of prepared formula a day, about 5 oz of powder (labels differ), × 10 days = 50 oz of powder. Ready-to-feed formula is safest in an emergency; powder needs safe water (counted in the water line). Check the amount every month as the baby grows. (AAP, CDC; some amounts are estimates)

Dry food for the dog for 10 days (at least a week): about 0.7 lb a day for each dog = 7 lb. Feed what the label says for yours, and keep it in an airtight, waterproof container. (ASPCA, Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)
Food for the dog for 10 days (10 pet-days, at least a week): what it eats now, in an airtight, waterproof container. (ASPCA, Ready.gov)

If you cook or boil water on a camp stove: about 0.2 lb of fuel a person a day × 3 people × 10 days = 6 lb, or 12 canisters of 0.5 lb each. Use it outdoors only, never indoors (carbon monoxide). (CDC, Ready Reckoner research, EIA, retail prices; some amounts are estimates)
Toilet paper: about 1 roll a person every 5 days × 2 people × 10 days = 4 rolls. Better still, measure a week's use and double it for two weeks. (Oregon OEM; some amounts are estimates)
Soap for 3 person-months: 3 people × 1 month. Each is 250 g of bathing soap and 200 g of laundry soap, about 1,350 g in all. (Sphere)

Period products for 2 cycles each, about 20 products a cycle (15 to 30). The form doesn't ask sex, so the plan counts half of the 2 people aged 13 to 64 who are not pregnant or nursing: 2 cycles' worth, about 40 products. Keep soap, clean underwear and pain relievers with them, and put used products in a separate bag. (CDC, Sphere, Oregon OEM; some amounts are estimates)
Diapers: about 8 a day for each baby (6 to 12; newborns use the most), × 10 days = 80 diapers. Keep at least one large pack on hand. (CDC, Sutter Health; some amounts are estimates)
Baby wipes: at least 2 packs for each child in diapers for up to 2 weeks: 2 packs. (CDC)

2 battery fans: 1 for the home plus 1 for the 1 person most at risk from heat (65 and over, babies, pregnancy). Fans help only while it is below 90 °F indoors; above that, go to a cooling centre. (CDC; some amounts are estimates)
3 cooling towels, one for each person: wet them and wear them on the neck in a heat wave. (an estimate)
A heat plan: find your nearest cooling centre (dial 2-1-1), pick the coolest room, cover sunny windows, and agree who checks on whom. Never leave people or pets in a closed car. (CDC, Ready.gov)
2 warm blankets, one for each person aged 1 and over: most homes already have them. Dress a baby in warm sleepwear or a sleep sack instead of loose blankets. (Ready.gov, Sphere, CDC)
3 sets of warm layers (coat, hat, gloves, dry socks), one for each person. (Ready.gov, CDC)

2 sleeping bags or extra heavy blankets, one for each person aged 1 and over, rated for the coldest nights where you live: your cold target of 5 days is longer than the 3 days that blankets and warm layers cover. (Ready.gov, Sphere; some amounts are estimates)

A cold plan: pick one room to keep warm, close off the others, put towels under doors and cover windows at night. Never heat with a gas oven, grill, camp stove or generator indoors (carbon monoxide). Gas, oil and propane furnaces usually need electricity for their fans and controls, so plan for cold without power. Babies under 1 should never sleep in a cold room. A body temperature below 95 °F needs medical help at once. (CDC; some amounts are estimates)

1 person takes prescription medicine every day: keep 14 days of it on hand. Keep a written list of each medicine, what it is for and the dose. After a disaster declaration some states let pharmacies give an emergency refill of up to 30 days, and many allow only a few days; ask your pharmacist what yours allows. (Florida DEM, CDC, Red Cross, Healthcare Ready)

1 person needs medicine kept cold, such as insulin: plan to keep it cool but never frozen for up to 7 days without power, with an insulated cooler and cold packs or ice you can replace. After 1 day without power, throw refrigerated medicine out unless its label says otherwise; ask your pharmacist how long yours can stay warm. (Ready.gov, CDC)

No antibiotics are included in this plan. If you have a specific, foreseeable need, such as remote travel, talk to your own clinician about a standby prescription with written instructions. Never use fish or pet antibiotics, never share prescriptions, and don't use expired ones. (CDC, FDA)
1 battery or hand-crank radio that gets NOAA Weather Radio, with a tone alert, for warnings when phones and power are down. (Ready.gov, NOAA)
Power banks: 2 phones × about 15 Wh a day (10 to 20) × 7 days without power = 210 Wh. Text instead of calling to save battery. (Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)

2 two-way radios for the 2 people aged 13 and over, to reach each other when phones are down. FRS radios need no licence; GMRS radios reach farther but need a $35 FCC licence that covers the family for 10 years. (FCC; some amounts are estimates)
2 written contact cards, one for each person aged 4 and over: an out-of-area contact, meeting places and key numbers. Phones die; paper does not. (Ready.gov)
1 paper map of your area, marked with meeting places and ways out. Save offline maps on your phone too. (Ready.gov)

Cash in small bills, kept with your documents, because ATMs and cards may not work in an outage: about $100 to start, or enough for about 3 days of basics (food, fuel, medicine) at your own daily spending. No agency gives a dollar amount. (Ready.gov, FEMA; some amounts are estimates)

2 go-bags, one for each person aged 4 and over (babies' things go in a parent's bag): a sturdy bag you already own will do. Pack copies of documents, a phone charger, cash, a flashlight, a whistle, a change of clothes and sturdy shoes, and add water, food and medicines from your home supplies rather than buying them twice. You may get only minutes of warning (a local tsunami or a fast fire), so keep the bags packed by the door, and one at work if you work in a danger zone. Practise grabbing them and leaving. Plan where you would stay for about 5 days. (Washington EMD, Ready.gov, CDC; some amounts are estimates)

Water for the go-bags comes out of the water you store at home, not on top of it: the Red Cross three-day supply for leaving home, about 5.5 gallons a day for the 3 people × 3 days = 16.5 gallons. Keep it with the bags or take it as you leave. If you leave on foot, carry what you can (about 2.5 L each) and a filter; the rest goes in the car. (Red Cross, Washington EMD, Ready.gov, CDC; some amounts are estimates)

Food for the go-bags comes out of your home food supply, not on top of it: about 4,523 kcal a day × 3 days = 13,600 kcal of food that needs no cooking or refrigeration. (Red Cross, Washington EMD, Dietary Guidelines)

1 pet carrier, one for each pet, with a pet go-kit: water and food from your home supplies, any medicine it takes, records and a photo. Public shelters may take only service animals, so find pet-friendly places to stay ahead of time. (ASPCA, Ready.gov)
Water for the pet go-kit, set aside from your stored water rather than bought extra: 7 days for the dog = 2.2 gallons. Replace it every 2 months. (ASPCA, PetMD; some amounts are estimates)
Food for the pet go-kit, set aside from your pet food rather than bought extra: 10 days (7 to 10 days) for the dog = 10 pet-days. Replace it every 2 months. (ASPCA)

Keep both vehicles at least half full at all times, and fill up when leaving looks likely. Keep an electric car at least half charged too, and charge it fully when a storm is forecast. (Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)

Person 1 travels 19.9 miles (32 km) by car to work or school; walking home at about 3 mph takes about 6.6 hours. Keep a get-home bag in the car: comfortable walking shoes, a light, a paper map, cash in small bills, a rain or warm layer, and water and snacks from home. Be ready to stay at work for 24 hours if you can't leave. (FHWA, Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)

Water for person 1's walk home: 6.6 hours × about 0.71 L an hour in heat = 4.7 L, in a bottle filled from home rather than bought extra. Past about 2.5 L, carry a filter or purification tablets and an empty bottle instead of all the water. (FHWA, NIOSH; some amounts are estimates)

Snacks for person 1's walk home: about 700 kcal for 6.6 hours on foot (about 1,250 kcal every 12 hours), from your food at home rather than bought extra. (FHWA, Dietary Guidelines; some amounts are estimates)

Person 2 travels 5 miles (8 km) by car to work or school; walking home at about 3 mph takes about 1.7 hours. Keep a get-home bag in the car: comfortable walking shoes, a light, a paper map, cash in small bills, a rain or warm layer, and water and snacks from home. Be ready to stay at work for 24 hours if you can't leave. (FHWA, Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)
Water for person 2's walk home: 1.7 hours × about 0.71 L an hour in heat = 1.2 L, in a bottle filled from home rather than bought extra. (FHWA, NIOSH; some amounts are estimates)

Snacks for person 2's walk home: about 200 kcal for 1.7 hours on foot (about 1,250 kcal every 12 hours), from your food at home rather than bought extra. (FHWA, Dietary Guidelines; some amounts are estimates)
2 car emergency kits: jumper cables, a flashlight, warm clothes, a blanket, bottled water and snacks; sand or cat litter in snow country. (Ready.gov)

1 family first-aid kit for 3 people: the Red Cross list for a family of 4 (bandages, gauze, tape, antiseptic wipes, gloves, a breathing barrier, a cold pack, tweezers, an emergency blanket and a thermometer). Add your own medicines and emergency numbers, and replace what you use. (Red Cross)

1 package of each of 4 kinds of non-prescription medicine (a pain reliever, an anti-diarrhea medicine, an antacid and a laxative): one package of each lasts about 14 days for 4 people. That is 4 packages for 10 days. Follow the label, and ask a pharmacist about children's versions. (Ready.gov, Red Cross; some amounts are estimates)

N95 masks for wildfire smoke or an outbreak: 1 a day for each of the 2 people aged 4 and over, for 5 days = 10 masks. A well-fitting N95 protects more than a cloth or surgical mask. (CDC, Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)
1 oral thermometer (non-mercury, non-glass; it is on the Red Cross kit list) and 1 infant thermometer for the baby. (Red Cross, CDC)

Oral rehydration salts for vomiting, diarrhea or heat illness: 3 packets a person for every 2 weeks, at least 2 weeks' worth. For 3 people and 14 days that is 9 packets. Mix each packet into 1 litre of safe water. (CDC; some amounts are estimates)

A fire escape plan: two ways out of every room, a meeting spot outside, and a practice run with everyone. If anyone sleeps upstairs, check that each bedroom has a second way out, such as a window onto a porch roof or an escape ladder. Test your smoke alarms every month. (Ready.gov)

No fire extinguisher yet: 2 multipurpose (A-B-C) extinguishers, one on each of the 2 floors a home like yours has, the ground-floor one near the kitchen. If your kitchen is on another floor, keep one there too. Learn how to use one before you need it. (USFA; some amounts are estimates)
Swap phone numbers with 2 neighbours and agree who checks on whom after a storm or an outage, when phones and roads may be down. (an estimate)

Savings goal: about 2.5 months of expenses ($17,500 at $7,000 a month), built up over time and kept apart from the supplies budget. You have about 4 months saved now. Planners often suggest 3 to 6 months; the CFPB says it depends on your situation. (FINRA, St. Louis Fed, CFPB)

Copy the 4 parts of FEMA's Emergency Financial First Aid Kit: IDs, financial and legal papers (including insurance), medical information, and household contacts. Keep copies in a waterproof, fire-resistant place or with someone you trust, with photos of your home and belongings, and update them once a year. (FEMA)

Home and renters policies usually don't cover floods. Decide on flood insurance before you need it: a new policy usually starts 30 days after you buy it. It pays up to $250,000 for the building and $100,000 for belongings. (FEMA, FloodSmart, Ready.gov)

packet_markdown:
# Your preparedness packet

**For:** 2 adults and 1 baby, with 1 dog  
**Where:** Fort Bend County, Texas (ZIP code 77479)  
**Home:** an owned house, with city water, gas heat and central air conditioning  
**Plan date:** October 1, 2026  
**Ready for:** serious disruptions, the kind that come about once in 50 years (the 1-in-50 setting), in the climate expected around 2050. Water is planned at the basic level, about 1 gallon a person a day.[1]

## Summary

**Where you are now:** getting started. **What is enough for your risks:** two weeks of supplies; each need stops at the step that covers it. At your budget, the plan gets there by month 3 (January 2027).

### The three things that matter most

1. Of 100 households like yours, about 75 (65–85) will lose grid power for a day or more in the next 10 years. Be ready to manage about 7 days at home with no power, and about 3 days with no tap water.
2. Of 100 households like yours, about 60 (40–90) will be unable to shop for food and supplies for 3 days or more in the next 10 years. Keep about 10 days of food you normally eat, and 2 weeks of daily medicine on hand.
3. Your longest targets come from one event the plan includes: a direct hit by a major hurricane. Planning for it changes: Power: 3 days → 7 days; Boil-water: 5 days → 7 days; Tap water: 2 days → 3 days; Food and supplies: 7 days → 10 days; Heat or cold: 3 days → 5 days; Medicine: 10 days → 14 days; Phone and payments: 2 days → 3 days; households like yours that have to leave home quickly within 10 years: 18 → 34 in 100. You can turn it off on the risks screen to see the plan without it.

### Start here

These cost nothing and come first. This month's 8 free steps are all under Your plan.

- [ ] Water and food know-how: boil water, use your water heater, keep food cold
- [ ] Keep medicines going: a written list, early refills, an emergency supply
- [ ] Tap water in clean reused bottles

### What the plan assumes you already have

- [x] A charged mobile phone: alerts, calls and a backup light (2 phones)
- [x] Go-bag for each person: a backpack you pack from your supplies (2 bags)
- [x] Manual can opener (1 opener)
- [x] A cooking pot with a lid (1 pot)
- [x] Three days of the food you normally eat (3 × 3 days of food for one person)
- [x] A warm blanket for each person (2 blankets)
- [x] Warm layers for each person: a coat, hat and gloves (3 sets)
- [x] Towels to wet and cool down (3 towels)

Most homes have these, so the plan does not ask you to buy them. If any is missing, untick "Assume everyday basics" on the Have screen, or list the item as not owned, and the plan will add it.

## Your risks

The events most likely to reach a household like yours in Fort Bend County, Texas, over the next 10 years, most likely first. A lost job or a week-long outage is far more likely than a disaster from the movies, and the plan is ordered the same way.

### The ones most likely to reach you

#### 1. Heat wave

Nearly every household like yours will go through a heat wave in a ten-year stretch around 2050 (about 1.5 times a year).[2, 3]

**What helps.** Know where you can go to cool off. Dial 2-1-1 to find air conditioning near you.[4] Cover windows with drapes or shades, and weather-strip doors and windows.[5] Take cool showers, wear loose, light-colored clothing, and drink plenty of fluids. Check on family members, older adults and neighbours.[5] Heat can cause power outages, so plan for refrigerated medicines and powered medical devices.[4] In a drought, follow local limits on water use, and make saving water a daily habit.[6]

**What to avoid.** Do not rely on a fan when it is over 90°F indoors. It can make you hotter.[4] Never leave people or pets in a closed car on a warm day. Heat stroke is an emergency. Signs include a body temperature above 103°F, hot, red, dry skin, a fast pulse and confusion. Call 911.[5]

**What it can do:** no power and dangerous heat or cold at home. **How bad:** Serious. **How sure:** Based on data.

#### 2. Medical emergency

Nearly every household like yours will have someone need emergency care in the next ten years (about 1.4 times a year).[7]

**What helps.** Take a first-aid and bleeding-control class. You may be able to save a life by acting right after an injury, before help arrives.[8] Keep a stocked first-aid kit. Check it regularly and replace anything used or out of date.[9] Keep a list of each person's medicines, doses and allergies with your emergency supplies.[10] Know how to reach 911. Call if you can, and text where that service works.[11] Set up telehealth with your own clinician before you need it.[12]

**What to avoid.** Do not start antibiotics on your own or take someone else's. The wrong medicine can delay the right treatment and cause serious side effects.[13] Do not use expired medicines.[14]

**What it can do:** a medical emergency. **How bad:** Serious. **How sure:** Based on data.

#### 3. Stranded in a vehicle

Of 100 households like yours, about 95 (63 to nearly all) will be stranded away from home by a crash, breakdown or shutdown in the next ten years.[15, 16]

**What helps.** Keep a car kit with jumper cables, sand, a flashlight, warm clothes, blankets, water and snacks.[17] Keep the gas tank at least half full.[18] Check the pressure in all your tires, including the spare, at least once a month.[19] Before a winter trip, tell someone where you are going and when you expect to arrive, and ask them to call for help if you are late.[20] If you drive an electric car, know its range and where you can charge along your route.[21, 22]

**What to avoid.** If you are stuck in a snowstorm, staying in the car is often safest. Tie a bright cloth to the antenna. Run the engine about 10 minutes an hour with a window open a little, and keep the exhaust pipe clear of snow.[20] Never drive into a flooded road or around the barriers.[23]

**What it can do:** being stranded away from home. **How bad:** Minor. **How sure:** Mostly data.

#### 4. Strong wind

Of 100 households like yours, about 90 (40 to nearly all) will lose power or have damage in a windstorm in the next ten years.[2, 16, 24, 25]

**What helps.** Pick your shelter spot now. A safe room or storm shelter is best. The next best is a small, windowless room or basement on the lowest floor of a sturdy building.[26] Sign up for your community's warnings, and learn what your sirens sound like.[26] Know the signs of a tornado: a rotating funnel cloud, a cloud of debris, or a roar like a freight train. In your shelter, protect your head and neck with your arms, and pile blankets or cushions around you.[26] When thunder roars, go indoors. Get into a building or a car with a roof.[27]

**What to avoid.** Stay away from windows, doors and outside walls.[26] There is no safe place in a car during a tornado, only less dangerous ones. If you are caught, stay buckled in and keep your head below the windows.[26] During a thunderstorm, avoid running water and electronics plugged into the wall.[27]

**What it can do:** no power, no phone, internet or card payments and damage to the home. **How bad:** Minor. **How sure:** Rough data.

#### 5. Supply chain disruption

Of 100 households like yours, about 86 (63–98) will find store shelves empty of things they need in the next ten years.[16]

**What helps.** Keep extra food that needs no refrigeration, cooking or water, and choose foods your family will eat.[28] Use the oldest cans first and replace them as you go.[29] Buy a little at a time. Ready.gov asks people to buy supplies slowly, so everyone can get what they need.[30] Keep a manual can opener.[28] The plan counts food in calories, not servings. Many "30-day" meal kits hold only about 1,300 to 1,700 calories a day.[31] That is less than most adults need.[32] Store food somewhere cool and dry. Below 85°F is best.[29]

**What to avoid.** Do not buy everything at once. It strains your budget and the store. Do not buy or eat from cans that bulge, leak, are rusted or are deeply dented.[29] Do not trust a kit's "days" label. Check the calories on the package instead.

**What it can do:** no way to get to a store and gaps in medicine. **How bad:** Minor. **How sure:** Expert estimate.

#### 6. Job loss

Of 100 households like yours, about 81 will have someone lose a job in the next ten years.[33, 34]

**What helps.** Build an emergency fund a little at a time. The right amount depends on your situation.[35] Planners often suggest three to six months of living expenses, and more if your income varies.[36] Know how to file for unemployment in your state.[37] Keep copies of your financial, legal and medical papers together, with the names of people to call.[38] Write a bare-bones budget you could switch to, and keep a pantry that can stretch a tight month.

**What to avoid.** Do not wait to file. Contact your state's unemployment program as soon as possible after losing work.[37] Do not keep your emergency fund in investments you would have to sell. A savings account lets you take money out at any time without a penalty.[36]

**What it can do:** lost income. **How bad:** Serious. **How sure:** Mostly data.

#### 7. Hurricane

Of 100 households like yours, about 63 (40–83) will lose power or have damage from a hurricane or tropical storm in a ten-year stretch around 2050.[16, 39, 40, 41]

**What helps.** Know your evacuation zone, your routes and where you would stay. If you live in a mandatory evacuation zone and officials tell you to leave, go right away.[42] Clear drains and gutters, bring in outdoor furniture, and think about storm shutters. Keep phones charged and have backup chargers.[42] A flood policy typically takes up to 30 days to start, so buy it well before a storm.[43] If you would leave in an electric car, keep it fully charged all hurricane season.[21]

**What to avoid.** Never walk or drive through floodwater. One foot of moving water can sweep a car away.[43] Do not drive or charge an electric car that has been in floodwater. Salt water can start a battery fire.[21] Never run a generator inside your home or garage.[44]

**What it can do:** no power, boil-water notices, no tap water, no way to get to a store, no phone, internet or card payments, having to leave home and damage to the home. **How bad:** Serious. **How sure:** Mostly data.

### Other risks we checked

| What could happen | Households like yours, the next 10 years | How bad | How sure |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Local water or gas outage | about 80 of 100[16, 45] | Minor | Mostly data |
| Cold wave | about 30 of 100[2] | Serious | Based on data |
| Long illness in the household | about 25 of 100[16] | Serious | Expert estimate |
| Chemical spill or release | about 25 of 100[16, 46] | Moderate | Mostly data |
| Cyberattack on services | about 20 of 100[16] | Minor | Expert estimate |
| Death or disability of an earner | about 15 of 100[16, 47, 48] | Very severe | Mostly data |
| Civil unrest | about 15 of 100[16] | Minor | Expert estimate |
| Pandemic | about 10 of 100[16, 49, 50] | Serious | Rough data |
| Ice storm | about 10 of 100[2, 16] | Moderate | Rough data |
| Winter storm | about 10 of 100[2, 16] | Minor | Rough data |
| Break-in | about 10 of 100[16] | Serious | Expert estimate |
| Lightning | about 7 of 100[16, 39] | Serious | Rough data |
| Regional blackout | about 5 of 100[16] | Moderate | Expert estimate |
| Drought | about 4 of 100[3, 16, 39] | Moderate | Rough data |
| Wildfire | about 4 of 100[3, 16, 39] | Moderate | Rough data |
| Flooding from rivers or heavy rain | about 4 of 100[3, 16, 51] | Very severe | Rough data |

### No grid power at home: about 7 days (5–10)

**What helps.** Have a flashlight for each person.[61] Keep a battery or hand-crank radio, and a backup battery for each phone.[62] Keep the fridge and freezer closed. A closed fridge keeps food cold for about four hours, and a full freezer for about two days.[61] If someone relies on a powered medical device or cold medicine, make a plan with their medical provider now.[61] You can also ask your power company to put you on its list for priority restoration.[10] A battery power station burns no fuel, so it makes no carbon monoxide.[44]

**What to avoid.** Never run a generator inside your home or garage, even with the doors and windows open. Keep it outside, more than 20 feet from windows, doors and vents.[44] Put a carbon monoxide alarm on every level of your home.[61] Never heat your home with a gas stove or oven. Unplug electronics, because the power can come back with a surge that damages them.[61]

### Tap water must be treated: about 7 days (5 days to 2 weeks)

**What helps.** Use bottled water, or bring clear water to a rolling boil for one minute. Boil for three minutes above 5,000 feet, then let it cool.[63] If you cannot boil water, add plain unscented bleach: 8 drops of 6% bleach or 6 drops of 8.25% bleach per gallon. Stir, and wait 30 minutes.[63] Use boiled or bottled water for drinking, cooking, brushing teeth, baby formula and ice. If the power is out too, a camp stove works, but only outdoors.[44]

**What to avoid.** Do not use water or ice from the fridge dispenser while a notice is on. Boil tap water even if it went through a home filter or a filter pitcher.[64] Boiling does not help if the notice warns of chemicals. That is a do-not-drink notice, and you need stored or bottled water instead.[64, 65]

### No tap water at all: about 3 days (2–10)

**What helps.** Store at least one gallon per person per day, for drinking and keeping clean.[1] Fill clean bottles or jugs with tap water and replace it every six months.[66] You can pick a level in the plan. About 3 liters a day covers drinking to survive, one gallon is the basic default, and about 4 gallons (15 liters) is the humanitarian minimum for drinking, cooking and washing.[67] A tank water heater holds 20 to 80 gallons of clean water.[68, 69] For long outages, a filter and a source of raw water go further than more jugs.[60] Filters do not remove viruses, so add a disinfectant such as chlorine dioxide after filtering.[65] A two-bucket toilet keeps waste safe when toilets cannot flush.[70]

**What to avoid.** Do not store water in containers that held chemicals.[66] Milk jugs seal poorly and turn brittle.[71] Never drink pool or spa water. Use it only for washing and cleaning.[69]

### Can't get to a store: about 10 days (7 days to 3 weeks)

**What helps.** See "Supply chain disruption" under Your risks.

### Dangerous heat or cold indoors: about 5 days (3–5)

**What helps.** Agree who checks on whom, especially older neighbours and anyone who lives alone.[4, 20] In heat, go where there is air conditioning. Dial 2-1-1 to find one.[4] Cover windows with drapes or shades.[5] In cold, close off rooms you don't need, stuff towels under doors, and cover windows with blankets at night. Have extra blankets, sleeping bags and warm coats.[20] Babies under one year old should never sleep in a cold room.[20]

**What to avoid.** Fans move air but do not lower body temperature.[5] Above 90°F indoors, a fan can make you hotter.[4] Never heat your home with a gas oven, and never use a grill or camp stove indoors.[44] Keep space heaters 3 feet from anything that can burn.[72] Never leave people or pets in a closed car on a warm day.[5]

### Medication and medical-supply continuity: about 2 weeks (10 days to 3 weeks)

**What helps.** Refill early, while you still have a week left. The Red Cross suggests keeping a 7-day supply, and Florida advises at least two weeks.[73, 74] People with diabetes should pack supplies for at least 1 to 2 weeks.[75] Talk to your doctor or pharmacist about building an emergency supply, and keep a written list of each person's medicines, doses and allergies.[10] Many states let pharmacists give an emergency refill, but the rules differ from state to state.[76] After a declared disaster, a federal program can help people without insurance replace prescriptions.[77] If a medicine must stay cold, ask how long it can be kept warm, and plan a cooler.[61]

**What to avoid.** If the power is out for more than a day, throw away medicine that should be refrigerated, unless the label says otherwise.[61] Keep insulin cool but never frozen.[78] Do not use expired medicines. Weak antibiotics can fail to treat an infection.[14] Do not share antibiotics or save them for later.[13]

### No phone, internet or card payments: about 3 days (2–5)

**What helps.** Turn on emergency alerts on every phone. They are free, and you do not need to sign up.[79] Keep a battery or hand-crank radio and a NOAA Weather Radio with a tone alert.[62] NOAA Weather Radio has more than 1,000 transmitters covering all 50 states.[80] Write important phone numbers on paper, not only in your phone.[81] Pick an out-of-state contact everyone can text, and a place to meet if you are separated.[82] Keep some cash in small bills, because ATMs and credit cards may not work.[83] License-free two-way radios (FRS) let family members talk over short distances without a phone network.[84]

**What to avoid.** Do not rely on one source of news. Do not assume you can text 911 everywhere. It is not available in every area, so call 911 if you can.[11]

**What to avoid.** Many people wait to check with others before they act on a warning.[85] Always follow the instructions of local officials, and leave early enough to avoid being trapped by bad weather.[18] Never walk or drive through floodwater. Six inches of moving water can knock you down.[43]

### House fire

**What helps.** Put smoke alarms inside and outside sleeping areas and on every level of your home. Test them every month.[86] Make an escape plan with two ways out of each room, and practice it twice a year.[87] Cooking left alone is the top cause of kitchen fires that spread beyond the pan, so stay with your cooking. Keep a pan lid or baking sheet nearby to cover a pan that catches fire.[88] Keep anything that can burn at least 3 feet from heaters, fireplaces and candles.[72] A multipurpose extinguisher labeled "A-B-C" works on most home fires.[89]

### Home and personal security

**What helps.** Burglars look for homes that are easy targets. **What to avoid.** After a disaster, be careful with people who show up offering fast repairs or help for a fee. Report scams at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.[94] Do not hide a spare key under the doormat or a planter. Leave it with a trusted neighbour.[90]

### Contacts and meeting places

- **Make a household plan and a contact card for each person.** Agree how you will reach each other, where you will meet if you are separated, and who picks up the children (Ready.gov). Pick one out-of-state contact everyone texts to say they are safe, since texts often get through when calls do not, and write key numbers on a card for each wallet or bag (Ready.gov). Add school, daycare and work plans, and go over the plan together once a year.[38, 81, 82, 101, 106, 107]
- **Set up emergency alerts and know how to reach 911.** Make sure every phone can get warnings: Wireless Emergency Alerts are free and need no sign-up (Ready.gov), but a phone only gets them when it is on, not in airplane mode, and served by a carrier that takes part (FCC). Add your county's text and email alerts and your power company's outage texts for local news. Call 911 when you can, because texting 911 works only in some places (FCC).[11, 61, 79, 106, 108]

### Leaving home: triggers and routes

About 35 of 100 households like yours have to leave home quickly at least once in 10 years. Warning can be 1 minute to 3 days ahead. Plan to be away for about 5 days.[3, 16, 39, 40, 41, 45, 46, 51, 52]

- **Plan how you would leave: zone, routes, destination and triggers.** Look up your evacuation zone and routes on your state and county emergency management websites, mark two routes on a paper map, and pick where you would go, pet-friendly if you have pets (Ready.gov). For each likely hazard, write a go-or-stay card and an if-then trigger, such as 'If our zone gets an evacuation warning, we leave within 30 minutes.' Plans written in if-then form make people more likely to follow through.[18, 42, 62, 85, 109, 110, 111, 112]
- **Keep your vehicle ready: half a tank, a charged battery, a good spare.** Keep at least half a tank of gas at all times and a full tank when an evacuation looks likely (Ready.gov); if you drive an electric car, keep it charged through storm season and pick destinations within its range (Hillsborough County, Florida). Check the spare tire with the others each month, and keep a phone charging cable in the car (NHTSA). Run the engine only outdoors, never in a garage (CDC).[17, 18, 19, 21, 22, 44, 99, 113]

- **Practice: ten-minute drills and the first things to do.**

#### Drills and if-then plans

**If-then plans.** An if-then plan links a trigger to an action: "If the county issues an evacuation warning for our zone, we leave within 30 minutes." Plans written this way help people follow through.[111] When a warning comes, people often wait to confirm it with others before they act.[85] A trigger you agreed on earlier leaves less to decide in the moment. Write one for each likely hazard, and add who picks up the children and where you will meet.[106]

**Drills.** In New Zealand, people who took part in earthquake drills knew the right actions better, used them more during real shaking, and did more to prepare.[114] Among people who got out of the World Trade Center on 9/11, those with earlier emergency training were less likely to develop PTSD.[115] Practice your fire escape plan twice a year.[87] Other ten-minute drills: Drop, Cover and Hold On, a night without power, grabbing the go-bag against a timer, and sealing a room to shelter in place.[112]

**What to avoid.** Do not skip drills because they feel silly. Each one you finish counts toward your plan.

#### Talking with children about emergencies

**Before anything happens.** Let children help build the kit and practice the plan.[116] Make sure each child knows your family meeting place and has a contact card.[106] Practice the fire escape plan together twice a year.[87]

**When something happens.** Start by asking what they already know and what questions they have. Give simple, concrete facts without scary details. For a young child, that might be: "A tree branch fell on the power lines, so the lights are off." Tell them about the many people working to help, and the steps being taken to keep them safe.[117]

**What to avoid.** Limit news coverage. If children watch, watch with them and answer their questions.[117] Reassure them when you honestly can, but do not give false reassurance. Let them know it is all right to be upset. If you feel overwhelmed, get support from another adult first. Helping others in the community can ease a child's sense of helplessness.[117]

### Neighbors

- **Neighbours and skills: swap numbers, check on each other, learn first aid.**

#### Neighbours and mutual aid

**The gap.** About 7 in 10 people expect help from friends and family in a disaster, but fewer than 2 in 10 had heard how to help their neighbours.[118]

**What helps.** Swap phone numbers with two neighbours. Agree who checks on whom, especially older neighbours and anyone who lives alone. Make a simple contact list for your street. Give a trusted person a spare key, and tell them where your supplies are and how to use any medical equipment.[119] Host a block party, since strong communities start with prepared neighbours.[120] Take CERT training to learn fire safety, light search and rescue, and disaster first aid.[121]

**What to avoid.** Do not wait for a disaster to meet the people next door. A short hello now makes it easier to knock on a door later.

### Pets

- **Pet plan: microchip, records, a photo and a buddy.** Keep your pet's ID tag and microchip details current, put vaccination records and a recent photo with your documents, and arrange a buddy who can care for or evacuate your pets if you cannot (Ready.gov). If officials ask you to evacuate, your pets should go too.[109, 110]

## Documents and money

Keep paper copies in a waterproof pouch and photos you can reach from any phone. FEMA's Emergency Financial First Aid Kit groups them in four parts.[38]

- [ ] **Who you are:** photo IDs, birth certificates, Social Security cards, passports, and pet records.
- [ ] **Money and legal papers:** insurance policies, the lease or deed, bank and card contact numbers (not PINs), and recent tax returns.
- [ ] **Medical papers:** insurance cards, the written medicine list, prescriptions, and vaccination records.
- [ ] **Contacts:** family, doctors, the insurance agent, the landlord or lender, and employers.

- **Documents and insurance: copy key papers, record belongings, check cover.** Use FEMA's Emergency Financial First Aid Kit to gather IDs, financial and legal papers, insurance, medical information and contacts, and photograph or video every room and valuable item. Keep paper copies in a waterproof bag and another copy with someone you trust or in secure online storage (FEMA). Check what your insurance covers: standard home and renters policies do not cover flood or earthquake damage, a new flood policy usually takes 30 days to start, and renters can buy their own policy and contents-only flood cover (Ready.gov, FEMA).[38, 43, 62, 82, 83, 118, 122, 123]
- **Fire-resistant, waterproof document pouch.** A fire-resistant, water-resistant pouch or small case for paper copies of key documents, a USB drive and some cash, easy to grab when you leave (FEMA's financial kit suggests fire- and waterproof storage).[38, 105]

### Insurance questions

- Home and renters policies usually don't cover floods. Decide on flood insurance before you need it: a new policy usually starts 30 days after you buy it. It pays up to $250,000 for the building and $100,000 for belongings. (FEMA, FloodSmart, Ready.gov)[83, 122, 123]

### Cash

- Cash in small bills, kept with your documents, because ATMs and cards may not work in an outage: about $100 to start, or enough for about 3 days of basics (food, fuel, medicine) at your own daily spending. No agency gives a dollar amount. (Ready.gov, FEMA; some amounts are estimates)[2, 16, 24, 25, 38, 39, 40, 41, 83, 99]

### Savings

Of 100 households like yours, about 15 (7–30) will have an income gap of more than 3 months in the next 10 years. The goal is about 2.5 months of expenses (about $17,500); you have 4 months saved. You already have enough saved for this goal. This is a savings goal, kept separate from the supplies budget.

- **Money: start an emergency fund and a bare-bones budget.** Set up an automatic transfer, however small, into a savings account you keep for emergencies; the CFPB says the right amount depends on your situation, and planners often suggest working toward three to six months of expenses (FINRA). Write down your essential monthly costs and what you would cut first, so you know how far savings would stretch. If anyone earns, find your state's unemployment website now, so you could file right away if a job ends (Department of Labor).[33, 35, 36, 37, 124, 125]

## Special needs

### Medicine

- 1 person takes prescription medicine every day: keep 14 days of it on hand. Keep a written list of each medicine, what it is for and the dose. After a disaster declaration some states let pharmacies give an emergency refill of up to 30 days, and many allow only a few days; ask your pharmacist what yours allows. (Florida DEM, CDC, Red Cross, Healthcare Ready)[16, 39, 40, 41, 45, 49, 50, 52, 73, 74, 75, 76, 96, 126]
- 1 person needs medicine kept cold, such as insulin: plan to keep it cool but never frozen for up to 7 days without power, with an insulated cooler and cold packs or ice you can replace. After 1 day without power, throw refrigerated medicine out unless its label says otherwise; ask your pharmacist how long yours can stay warm. (Ready.gov, CDC)[2, 16, 24, 25, 39, 40, 41, 61, 78, 96, 127]

- **Keep medicines going: a written list, early refills, an emergency supply.** Write a paper list of each person's medicines with the dose their prescriber set, allergies, and the prescriber's and pharmacy's numbers, and keep copies in the go-bag and with your documents (Ready.gov). If anyone takes a daily medicine, refill when a week is left and ask the prescriber and pharmacist how to build an emergency supply; some states allow emergency refills, and a federal program can help people without insurance after a disaster. Set up telehealth and pharmacy logins now, and put spare glasses in the go-bag (Ready.gov).[10, 12, 14, 38, 62, 73, 76, 77, 126]
- **Insulated bag and cold packs for refrigerated medicine.** An insulated bag with cold packs to keep medicine such as insulin cool, but never frozen, when the power is out or you have to leave. Ready.gov advises throwing out refrigerated medicine after a day without power unless its label says otherwise, so ask your pharmacist how long yours lasts.[61, 78, 105]

### Antibiotics

- No antibiotics are included in this plan. If you have a specific, foreseeable need, such as remote travel, talk to your own clinician about a standby prescription with written instructions. Never use fish or pet antibiotics, never share prescriptions, and don't use expired ones. (CDC, FDA)[13, 14, 128, 129]

### Babies and toddlers

- 1 baby on formula: up to 32 oz of prepared formula a day, about 5 oz of powder (labels differ), × 10 days = 50 oz of powder. Ready-to-feed formula is safest in an emergency; powder needs safe water (counted in the water line). Check the amount every month as the baby grows. (AAP, CDC; some amounts are estimates)[2, 16, 39, 40, 41, 49, 50, 99, 130, 131, 132, 133]
- Diapers: about 8 a day for each baby (6 to 12; newborns use the most), × 10 days = 80 diapers. Keep at least one large pack on hand. (CDC, Sutter Health; some amounts are estimates)[2, 16, 39, 40, 41, 49, 50, 99, 131, 133, 134]
- Baby wipes: at least 2 packs for each child in diapers for up to 2 weeks: 2 packs. (CDC)[2, 16, 39, 40, 41, 49, 50, 131, 133]
- 1 oral thermometer (non-mercury, non-glass; it is on the Red Cross kit list) and 1 infant thermometer for the baby. (Red Cross, CDC)[9, 131]

- **Pack an infant go-kit from CDC's checklist.** Use CDC's emergency checklist for families with infants: formula or breastfeeding supplies, diapers and wipes, an infant thermometer, a bulb syringe, a pain reliever made for infants, warm sleepwear or a sleep sack, and a portable crib. Babies under one should never sleep in a cold room (CDC).[20, 131]

### Pets and animals

- Dry food for the dog for 10 days (at least a week): about 0.7 lb a day for each dog = 7 lb. Feed what the label says for yours, and keep it in an airtight, waterproof container. (ASPCA, Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)[2, 16, 39, 40, 41, 49, 50, 99, 109, 110, 133]
- 1 pet carrier, one for each pet, with a pet go-kit: water and food from your home supplies, any medicine it takes, records and a photo. Public shelters may take only service animals, so find pet-friendly places to stay ahead of time. (ASPCA, Ready.gov)[18, 110]
- Water for the pet go-kit, set aside from your stored water rather than bought extra: 7 days for the dog = 2.2 gallons. Replace it every 2 months. (ASPCA, PetMD; some amounts are estimates)[99, 110, 135]
- Food for the pet go-kit, set aside from your pet food rather than bought extra: 10 days (7 to 10 days) for the dog = 10 pet-days. Replace it every 2 months. (ASPCA)[110]

### Stress and mental health

#### Stress, mental health and the 988 line

**What helps.** Save 988 in every phone. It offers free, judgment-free support 24/7 for mental health, substance use and more, by call, text or chat.[136] After a disaster, the Disaster Distress Helpline offers crisis counseling 24/7 to anyone in emotional distress. Call or text 1-800-985-5990.[137] Write a short calm plan: what you might feel, what helps you, and who you will call.[112] Oregon's 2 Weeks Ready program even includes practicing mindfulness as a step in getting prepared.[138]

**What to avoid.** Do not keep the news on all day. No one, adult or child, benefits from graphic details or disturbing images.[117] Do not wait until things feel unbearable to reach out. The 988 line supports people in emotional distress as well as in crisis.[136]
